# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Research rarely unfolds as a single fixed analysis. Researchers inspect data as they accumulate, reconsider recruitment in the light of interim results, stop early when an effect looks convincing, and initiate follow-up studies because earlier findings looked promising. Conventional fixed-horizon testing, by contrast, asks the researcher to specify the sample size and analysis plan before the data are examined, and its type-I error guarantee holds when that procedure is followed. Classical statistics also offers group-sequential and alpha-spending methods for planned interim monitoring [@obrien1979multiple; @lan1983discrete]. What fails is the unadjusted reuse of a fixed-horizon rule. Repeatedly recomputing the same fixed-horizon p-value and stopping at the first favourable result offers more chances to cross a fixed threshold and can drive the false-positive probability far above its nominal level [@ly2025savi; @ramdas2023gametheoretic]. A fresh follow-up study can still be analysed validly on its own. The difficulty arises at the level of a study series when decisions to launch, continue, publish or combine studies depend on earlier results, which can create accumulation bias [@terschure2019accumulation]. More broadly, misuse of p-values, selective analysis and incomplete reporting have been identified as significant contributors to concerns about reproducibility [@wasserstein2016asa]. One response proposed lowering the conventional significance threshold for claims of new discoveries [@benjamin2018redefine].

E-values and safe testing address these problems directly. Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the null hypothesis. Following the terminology of @vovk2021evalues and the formal treatment of @ramdas2024hypothesis, an e-variable for $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-negative random variable satisfying
$$
\mathbb{E}_P[E] \leq 1
\qquad
\text{for every } P \in \mathcal{P}.
$$
Its realised value after observing the data is called an e-value, and large values count as evidence against the null. Markov's inequality turns the rule "reject when $E \geq 1/\alpha$" into a level-$\alpha$ test, so at the five per cent level an e-value of twenty warrants rejection.

As data accumulate, conditionally valid one-step e-variables, each evaluated on fresh information given the past, can be multiplied to form a test supermartingale. Every test supermartingale is an e-process, so its value at any stopping time remains a valid e-variable. Ville's inequality bounds the probability that a non-negative supermartingale with initial expectation at most one ever crosses a given level by the reciprocal of that level [@ville1939; @ramdas2023gametheoretic]. This is a statement about the whole path rather than one pre-chosen sample size, and it yields anytime-validity, meaning that the error guarantee holds uniformly over stopping times.

An analyst may therefore monitor continuously and stop when the evidence is convincing. Evidence can also be continued across later stages or studies without spending the error budget twice, provided that each new stage contributes a conditionally valid e-variable for the same null, evaluated on fresh data [@grunwald2024safe; @ramdas2024hypothesis]. Optional stopping preserves validity at the chosen stopping time, while optional continuation preserves validity through the product of these conditionally valid contributions. These are the forms of flexibility that defeat an unadjusted fixed-horizon analysis.

Every e-value has a frequentist interpretation through its error bound and a betting interpretation as realised wealth against the null. For e-values constructed as likelihood ratios or Bayes factors, the same number also has a model-comparison interpretation. The betting view is especially useful. An e-value records how much a pre-specified stake against the null has multiplied, and the expectation bound says that the bettor cannot make a systematic profit when the null holds. These ideas are developed in the safe-testing framework of @grunwald2024safe, with a broader rethinking of the goals of testing in @grunwald2024beyond and a systematic treatment in @ramdas2024hypothesis. They build on the martingale foundations going back to Ville and the game-theoretic view of probability associated with Shafer and Vovk [@shafer2021testing; @ramdas2023gametheoretic].

Even so, e-values have not yet become a standard tool in applied statistics, and practitioner-oriented material remains less abundant than theoretical work. The framework is recent, its conventions reverse familiar p-value habits, and complete worked analyses in the e-value idiom remain relatively scarce. Two recent works address this from opposite directions. @ramdas2024hypothesis give a systematic treatment at research level, and @ly2025savi give a tutorial for practitioners, organised around sample-size planning and worked largely in the t-test setting, which prioritises readability for an applied audience over rigorous mathematical presentation and defers the latter to specialised works. This thesis sits between them: it keeps the derivations that a tutorial defers, at a level a master's student can follow, and covers material that practitioner-oriented treatments have so far left aside, including safe counterparts of four standard tests, the e-process machinery behind optional stopping and continuation, and false discovery rate control with e-values.

It is intended as a practical guide to e-values for statistics students and for the practitioners they go on to become. The contribution is one of accessibility rather than novelty, and no new theorems are claimed. The guide offers a route into the subject from first principles and explains how the methods are realised in software through the `safestats` R package [@turner2022safestats]. All code underlying the analyses and simulations in this thesis is available at <https://github.com/KilianG01/evalues-thesis>. One qualification matters throughout: the word "safe" names a precise technical guarantee, not an unconditional assurance. The guarantee is relative to the stated null model and to the assumptions of the construction being used, including correct model specification, a limitation emphasised in the published discussion of the safe-testing framework [@pawel2024safetestingdiscussion].

The rest of the thesis follows the natural development of the subject. It opens with the foundations of e-values, setting out the distinction between e-variables and their realised e-values, the sense in which they are valid, and the complementary readings of evidence through likelihood ratios and betting. It then specialises the idea to the standard testing problems an applied statistician meets, building safe counterparts of the z-test, the t-test, the test for two proportions and the logrank test through the `safestats` package. From there it turns to the sequential core of the theory, taking in test supermartingales, e-processes, optional stopping and Ville's inequality, together with the confidence sequences that accompany anytime-valid tests and the product construction for combining conditionally valid contributions across stages. A later chapter takes up multiple testing with e-values, including the eBH procedure [@wang2022fdr] and the e-Partitioning Principle for false discovery rate control [@goeman2025epartitioning]. The main body closes with a case study applying these methods to a real randomised clinical trial, the ACTG 175 study of antiretroviral therapies [@hammer1996trial], alongside an analysis of the BCG vaccination trials that illustrates optional continuation across separate studies. A final discussion chapter draws together the main conclusions, limitations and directions for future work. In keeping with the character of a guide, the review of prior work is woven in rather than set apart. There is no separate survey chapter, and each chapter opens by citing the specific work it builds on, so that methods and sources are introduced together at the point where they are needed.
